options.text: hello! The method deletes every x or y anywhere in the string, including the middle.
options.feedback: strip trims boundaries, not interior positions. The x and y inside hexyllo! remain, so the output is hexyllo!, not hello!.

options.text: hexyllo! The argument is the exact substring xy, which strip removes once from each end when present.
options.feedback: The output is right here, but the argument is not an exact substring. It specifies individual characters x and y to trim repeatedly from either boundary in any order. The middle stays unchanged.

options.text: xyhexyllo! The method trims matching characters only from the right end.
options.feedback: strip works at both ends. It removes the initial x and y as well as the final y and x, stopping at h on the left and ! on the right. The result is hexyllo!.

options.text: hexyllo! The argument supplies individual characters x and y to trim repeatedly from both ends, without removing interior characters.
options.feedback: Correct. Both boundary runs contain only x and y, so they are removed. Trimming stops at h and !, leaving the interior xy untouched.

options.text: xyhexyllo!xy The method removes only whitespace, ignoring its argument, so this string is unchanged.
options.feedback: Whitespace trimming is the default when no character argument is supplied. Here the explicit argument selects x and y, so those boundary characters are removed and hexyllo! is printed.

explanation: strip's argument is a collection of individual characters, not a prefix or suffix string. Starting at each boundary, it removes x and y until a different character is reached. The boundaries xy disappear, but the interior xy between he and llo! remains. The printed result is hexyllo!. Exact-substring removal happens to predict this example too, but is not the general strip rule.
